question: Are you an exterminator?

children.text: No. We're a wildlife removal company, not an exterminator, and we don't spray. For rats, raccoons, squirrels or bats, we find how they get in, remove them the way Florida law allows and seal the entry points. If you were searching for wildlife exterminators, this is the work you're after.

question: How much does wildlife removal cost in Central Florida?

children.text: It depends on the animal, how many there are, how many entry points need sealing and how high or hard to reach they are. A single raccoon caught in a yard is a different job from a bat colony in a tile roof. We give you the price for your home after the inspection, before any work starts.
The inspection is free.

question: How fast can you come out?

children.text: Same-day appointments are often available. For an animal loose inside the living space, a snake in the house or bees near people, tell us when you call so we can treat it as urgent.

question: Is your wildlife removal humane?

children.text: Yes. We use one-way doors that let animals leave and not come back, live traps that are checked at least every 24 hours as Florida law requires, and removal by hand. Mothers and young are kept together. We never use poison on bats, which is illegal in Florida.

question: Can I trap and move the animal myself?

children.text: Florida allows a property owner to trap many nuisance animals, but the rules are strict. Traps must be checked at least every 24 hours. A native animal can be released on the same property, or on land of at least 40 contiguous acres in the same county with the landowner's written permission. Non-native animals can't be released at all. Bats can't be trapped or relocated. Those rules are why many people hand the job to wildlife trappers like us, whether it's an armadillo under the slab or a possum in the garage.
New FWC trapping rules start December 31, 2026.
They change trap check times, allow remote (camera) checks, and require most people who trap to complete FWC's annual registration and training, which FWC says is
at no cost

. A homeowner using one regular-size cage trap (door up to 20 by 28 inches) on their own property, to catch nuisance or non-native wildlife, doesn't need registration, training or reporting. Nuisance animals moved off site must be released or put down within 12 hours of the trap check, down from 24. Details at
MyFWC.com/TrappingRules

question: Do you seal the entry points?

children.text: Yes. Removing the animal without closing the hole just makes room for the next one. After the animals are out, we close the openings they used and the weak spots around them.

question: Another company already tried. Why are the animals still getting in?

children.text: Usually because an opening was missed. UF/IFAS says rodent-proofing only works if every possible entry is blocked, and that rats probe new repairs in the first couple of weeks. Trapping without sealing just makes room for the next animal. We start with the whole roofline and attic, not just the hole you found.
Before you hire anyone, ask what the quote covers: every opening on the house, or only the one in use today.

question: Is it safe to sweep up droppings in the attic myself?

children.text: No. The CDC says not to sweep or vacuum rodent droppings, because that can put germs in the air. Its steps are gloves, a disinfectant or bleach soak, then paper towels. We'll point out where the droppings and soiled insulation are during the inspection.

question: Is it legal to remove bats from my house in Florida?

children.text: Yes, by exclusion, outside maternity season. From August 15 to April 15, one-way devices can be used to let bats leave and keep them out. Killing, trapping, relocating or poisoning bats is illegal at any time of year.

question: When is bat maternity season in Florida?

children.text: April 16 through August 14. That's when most Florida bats give birth and raise pups that can't fly yet. Excluding the adults then would leave the pups to die inside, so exclusion isn't allowed in that window without an FWC permit.

question: I have bats in June. What can I do?

children.text: Call for an inspection anyway. We can confirm it's bats, find all the openings, seal the ones the bats aren't using and put you first in line for August 15. Keep doors to the attic closed and don't try to block the bats' exit yourself.

question: Can I just seal the hole the bats use?

children.text: Not while bats are inside. FWC warns that bats that don't get out before their exit is sealed die inside the building. Sealing comes after the one-way doors have done their job.

question: How long does bat exclusion take?

children.text: The one-way devices stay up for at least four nights with lows of 50°F or warmer, as FWC requires, and often longer until no bats are left. Then the openings are sealed.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: how long a typical bat job takes from first visit to final sealing]

question: What kind of bats live in Central Florida homes?

children.text: FWC describes the Brazilian free-tailed bat as a bat commonly found in Florida buildings. Evening bats tuck into tight spots too, even the folds of a closed patio umbrella.

question: There's one bat in my living room. Do I have a colony?

children.text: Not necessarily. A single bat can fly in through an open door, and FWC allows one bat in the living space to be removed at any time of year: close it into one room and open a window so it can leave. But if anyone may have touched it, or someone woke up with it in the room, the CDC says to call your county health department before letting it go, so it can be tested. If bats keep showing up, or you see them leave the roof at dusk, there's a roost.

question: Will a bat house get them out of my attic?

children.text: No. FWC says a bat house isn't a substitute for exclusion. But it can help: put one up before the exclusion starts, close to the roost and in the bats' flight path, on a pole or a building rather than a tree, so the colony has somewhere else to go.

question: Looking for a rat exterminator near me?

children.text: Pro Wildlife Removal is a rat removal company rather than an exterminator, and there's no spraying. We find the openings the rats use, trap the ones inside and seal those entry points, so the house is closed to the next ones. Call (844) 264-6254.

question: Are they roof rats or Norway rats?

children.text: In an attic, almost always roof rats. Florida DOH describes roof rats as good climbers that nest in trees and plants but generally like high places such as attics, with a tail longer than the body. Norway rats burrow under buildings and beneath concrete slabs. UF/IFAS adds that Norway rats are heavier and found mainly along Florida's coasts and canals. Florida DOH says the two sometimes live together, though roof rats like to be up high. More in
Norway rat vs roof rat

question: How small a hole can a rat get through?

children.text: UF/IFAS says a rat can squeeze through a crack half an inch wide, and a mouse through a quarter inch. Rats can also climb wires and pipes, and jump from a branch to a roof. See
how big of a hole does a rat need

question: Why do the rats keep coming back after I trap them?

children.text: Because the way in is still open. Trapping removes the rats inside, and new ones find the same gaps. The openings have to be sealed with materials rats can't chew.

question: Should I put out poison?

children.text: We don't recommend it as a first step. UF/IFAS Extension calls rodenticides a last resort, to be used only in tamper-resistant stations away from children and pets. Poison also does nothing about the holes.

question: I saw a rat during the day. Is that bad?

children.text: Usually it means more rats than you think. Rats are most active at night, and UF/IFAS says rodents seen again and again by day point to an established population. Florida DOH says Norway rats come out in daylight when numbers are high, when they're disturbed, or when their food source is threatened. UF/IFAS has also linked daytime sightings to sick or poisoned rats.

question: How long does it take to get rid of rats?

children.text: The sealing is usually done first, then the trapping runs until no more rats are caught and no new signs show up. UF/IFAS advises checking the seals often in the first two weeks, when rats look for weak spots.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: how long a typical rat job takes]

question: Is it safe to clean up rat droppings myself?

children.text: For a few droppings, follow the CDC's steps: air the space out for 30 minutes, wear gloves, soak the droppings in disinfectant or 1 part bleach to 9 parts water, wait five minutes, then wipe them up with paper towels. Never sweep or vacuum them. For a whole attic, call us.

question: Can I catch the rat alive and let it go?

children.text: No. Rats aren't native to Florida, and FWC doesn't allow non-native animals to be released. UF/IFAS Extension also advises against live-trapping and releasing rats.

question: Do I need a raccoon exterminator?

children.text: No. A raccoon in the attic is a wildlife job, not an exterminator's. It's removed under FWC's rules, babies included, and the hole it used is sealed. That's the work we do, with no spraying involved.

question: When do raccoons have babies in Florida?

children.text: UF/IFAS says births in Florida generally happen in March and April, with an average litter of 3 to 4 young and as many as 7. That's why spring is the busiest time for raccoons in attics.

question: Can I trap the raccoon and take it somewhere else?

children.text: Not just anywhere. Florida allows release on the property where it was caught, or on at least 40 contiguous acres in the same county with the landowner's written permission. Releasing it anywhere else, like a park, is illegal, and a set trap has to be checked at least once every 24 hours.

question: Why not just close the hole while the raccoon is out at night?

children.text: If there are kits inside, they're cut off from their mother. Even without kits, Purdue Extension notes a raccoon will likely try to get back into an attic it treats as its den, and you have to be absolutely sure it's out before you close anything. Check first.

question: Are raccoons dangerous?

children.text: They usually avoid people, but they're wild animals that bite and scratch when cornered. Raccoons are one of the main wildlife sources of rabies in Florida, and their droppings can carry roundworm. Keep pets and children away and let us handle it.

question: How do I clean up raccoon droppings in my yard?

children.text: FWC and the CDC both advise wearing gloves, removing the droppings promptly and burning or burying them, or bagging them for the landfill. The CDC suggests boiling water or a propane flame-gun on decks and patios. Wash your hands afterwards. For an attic latrine, call us.

question: How do I keep raccoons from coming back?

children.text: Close the entry with strong materials, cap the chimney, trim branches back from the roof, and don't leave pet food or unsecured trash out at night. Florida law prohibits placing food in a way that attracts raccoons. See
what to do about raccoons

question: Can you come out at night for a raccoon in the house?

children.text: Same-day visits are often available for a raccoon loose in the house. If it's inside the living space, tell us when you call.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: night and weekend response for a raccoon loose in the living space]

question: How do I know it's squirrels and not rats?

children.text: Timing is the easiest clue. Gray squirrels keep daylight hours. Noise after dark points to rats, or to flying squirrels, which come out at night. See
squirrel insulation damage
for what they do inside.

question: When do squirrels have babies in Florida?

children.text: FWC says Florida's squirrels tend to breed twice a year, with litters in spring and autumn. Litters average one to four young.

question: A squirrel got into my house. What do I do?

children.text: FWC's advice: move your pets to another part of the house, then open an outside door or window in that room so the squirrel can find its own way out.

question: Can I trap the squirrel and release it at a park?

children.text: No. Florida allows release only on the property where it was caught, or on 40 acres or more in the same county with the landowner's written permission. Releasing it somewhere else isn't legal.

question: Why do squirrels keep coming back after removal?

children.text: Because the roof still has a way in. Squirrels chew through soft patches and find the next weak spot. The fix is sealing every opening properly. Read
why squirrels return after removal

question: Will trimming my trees help?

children.text: Yes. FWC recommends keeping tree limbs trimmed well back from the roof so squirrels can't step straight onto it. It won't stop a squirrel that's already inside, but it helps keep the next one off.

question: Do you remove flying squirrels too?

children.text: Yes. The southern flying squirrel is one of Florida's three native squirrels, and it's also treated as a nuisance animal when it gets into a building. Read about
flying squirrels in Florida

question: How many venomous snakes are in Florida?

children.text: Six of Florida's 50 snake species are venomous, according to FWC: the eastern diamondback rattlesnake, timber rattlesnake, dusky pygmy rattlesnake, cottonmouth, eastern coral snake and southern copperhead. In Central Florida, the four to know are the diamondback, pygmy rattlesnake, cottonmouth and coral snake.

question: How do I tell a coral snake from a kingsnake?

children.text: Look at where the red is. On the venomous coral snake, the red rings touch the yellow rings, and the nose is black. On the harmless scarlet kingsnake, the red touches black, and the nose is red. If you're not sure, treat it as venomous and keep away.

question: What do I do if someone is bitten?

children.text: Call 911. UF/IFAS's snakebite plan says to get away from the snake, keep the bitten arm or leg still, in a comfortable, neutral position (the CDC's current wording), remove rings and watches, and wash the bite with soap and water. Don't use a tourniquet, ice, cutting or suction, and don't try to catch the snake. You don't need to identify it for treatment. The Poison Control hotline is 1-800-222-1222.

question: There's a snake in my garage. What do I do?

children.text: UF/IFAS suggests closing the door between the garage and the house and opening the outside doors so the snake can leave on its own. Keep pets and children away. If it doesn't leave, or you can't tell what it is, call us.

question: Why do I keep finding snakes around my house?

children.text: Usually food or cover. FWC says frequent snake sightings near a house can mean rodents. Clear brush and debris piles, clean up spilled bird seed and pet food, and check for rats. See
types of animals found under the house

question: Do snake repellents work?

children.text: No. UF/IFAS says the products sold as snake repellents simply do not work. Sealing gaps and removing food and cover does.

question: Can you come right away for a snake in the house?

children.text: Same-day visits are often available for a snake inside. Tell us it's inside and where, and keep the room closed off until we get there.

question: Do you handle possum control in Tampa?

children.text: Yes. Opossum control in Tampa works the same as anywhere else we cover: find where the possum gets in under the house, the deck or into the attic, get it out, young included, and close the opening with wire mesh. Call (844) 264-6254.

question: Do opossums carry rabies?

children.text: It's rare. UF/IFAS describes opossums as nearly immune to rabies. In Florida, rabies mostly comes from raccoons and bats, but wash any animal bite or scratch and see a doctor. A frightened opossum hisses, growls and may bite, so don't handle one.

question: I saw an opossum in the daytime. Is it sick?

children.text: Not necessarily. FWC says opossums are mostly nocturnal but may be active during the day, which is normal behavior and not by itself a sign of illness.

question: The opossum looks dead. What do I do?

children.text: It may be playing dead. FWC says not to pick it up. Leave it alone, or gently move it to a quiet spot with a shovel, and it will probably get up and leave on its own within minutes to a few hours.

question: When do opossums have babies in Florida?

children.text: UF/IFAS says most young are born between February and June, though breeding can continue into November. UF/IFAS says females usually have one or two litters a year, and FWC says the young ride on their mother's back once they leave the pouch at about 80 days.

question: Can I trap the opossum and take it to the woods?

children.text: Only to land you're allowed to use. Florida lets a trapped opossum be released on the property where it was caught, or on 40 acres or more in the same county with the landowner's written permission. Traps have to be checked at least once a day.

question: How do I keep opossums from coming back?

children.text: Take away food and shelter. Secure trash and pet food, pick up fallen fruit, and once you know the opossum is out, block the openings under the house with wire mesh. FWC suggests a motion-activated sprinkler at the entrance to discourage one from going back in.

question: Can I get leprosy from an armadillo?

children.text: It's possible but very unlikely. The CDC says some armadillos naturally carry the bacteria, but the risk is very low and most people who come into contact with armadillos are unlikely to get leprosy. As a simple precaution, wear gloves if you ever have to touch one.

question: Why is an armadillo digging up my lawn?

children.text: It's hunting. Armadillos dig for grubs, earthworms and insect larvae, and FWC says moist soil and lush, fertilized lawns bring those closer to the surface. Water less, water in the morning, and ease off the fertilizer.

question: Do armadillo repellents work?

children.text: UF/IFAS says no chemical repellents or fumigants are registered for armadillos in Florida, and poison baits are illegal and don't work. FWC suggests shining a bright light into the burrow or putting a radio near it, without blocking the exit, to encourage the animal to move on.

question: Can I trap the armadillo and move it?

children.text: Only to land the rules allow. FWC lets a trapped armadillo be released on the property where it was caught, or on 40 contiguous acres or more in the same county with the owner's written permission, and calls relocation seldom biologically sound. Traps must be checked every 24 hours.

question: Can an armadillo damage my foundation?

children.text: UF/IFAS says burrows under driveways and patios can cause structural damage. If a burrow runs under a slab, get the armadillo out and the burrow filled before it settles. Wire laid along the foundation helps stop new digging.

question: When do armadillos have babies?

children.text: UF/IFAS says armadillos breed in summer but don't give birth until spring. FWC adds that a female has identical quadruplets: one egg splits into four young of the same sex.

question: There's a swarm of bees on my tree. Will it leave?

children.text: Often, yes. UF/IFAS says swarms are temporary and stay a few hours to a few days, and they're usually calm. Keep people and pets away and don't disturb it. If it starts building comb or is still there after a few days, it's becoming a colony: call us.

question: Can I spray the bees myself?

children.text: UF/IFAS says untrained people should never disturb a colony. Killing a colony counts as pest control in Florida and has to be done by a licensed pest control operator. Leave it to a professional.

question: Can I just seal the hole the bees use?

children.text: No. UF/IFAS warns that sealing an active opening forces the bees further into the wall and possibly into your home. The colony and comb have to come out first.

question: What do I do if bees attack?

children.text: UF/IFAS says run in a straight line to shelter, cover your face as you go, and get inside a house, shed or car. Don't jump into water, don't hide in bushes and don't swat. Call 911 if someone is being attacked. Pull stingers out as fast as you can: the method doesn't matter.

question: Are the bees at my house African honey bees?

children.text: Assume they could be. UF/IFAS says African bees have been in Florida since 2001 and hybridize with European honey bees, and the hybrids show an unpredictable mix of both kinds of behavior. Treat any colony in Central Florida with care.

question: Do you remove bees in Pasco and Hillsborough County?

children.text: Yes. We take bee swarm and beehive calls across Pasco and Hillsborough counties and the six other Central Florida counties we serve. Call (844) 264-6254.

question: Why does the honeycomb have to come out?

children.text: UF/IFAS says comb left in a wall can melt and stain it, the honey ferments and the brood rots, and wax moths and beetles move in. Removing the whole nest is part of the job.

question: How long does a dead animal smell last?

children.text: It depends on the animal's size, where it is and the heat. A larger animal in a hot attic lasts far longer than a mouse in a cool crawl space. Removing it is the only way to end it quickly.

question: Can you find an animal inside a wall?

children.text: Usually, yes. We trace the smell, flies and staining to the spot, then open the smallest area needed. We'll tell you before any cutting.

question: Is it dangerous to be around a dead animal?

children.text: The CDC says the risk from animal carcasses is low if you take proper precautions: gloves, bagging the remains and washing your hands. Don't touch one bare-handed, and keep children and pets away.

question: How do I dispose of a dead cat or dog in my yard?

children.text: The CDC's disposal steps for dead animals apply: wear gloves, slip a plastic bag over your hand, pick the animal up, turn the bag inside out and seal it, and use a shovel for a larger animal. Its guidance also says to call animal control. Wash your hands afterwards. If the animal is somewhere you can't reach, call (844) 264-6254.

question: What if it's a bat?

children.text: Don't throw it away, and don't touch it. The CDC says to contact animal control or your health department to capture a bat for testing, not to release it, and to report any contact. If it's already dead, Florida's Department of Health asks that the head not be damaged.

question: Do you remove dead animals from under the house or in the yard?

children.text: [PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: confirm the places you remove dead animals from (crawl spaces, under decks and sheds, attics, walls, vents, yards, engine bays)]
If it's on a public road, call your city or county instead.

question: Will you find out why it died in my house?

children.text: We'll find how it got in. Animals that die in attics and walls are often rats, squirrels or bats that were living there, so we check for others and for the open gap.

question: Why are rats in my attic?

children.text: Shelter, close to food and water. Florida DOH says roof rats nest in trees and plants but generally like high places such as attics. UF/IFAS says rats climb wires, pipes, vines and trees to get into a building. Fruit trees, pet food and bird seed nearby help.

question: How long can rats live in an attic?

children.text: As long as the way in stays open. UF/IFAS gives a roof rat's life span as about a year, but the colony keeps going as young rats grow up. See
how long rats can live in an attic

question: Will the rats leave on their own?

children.text: Not while the attic gives them shelter and the gap stays open. The attic has to be sealed and the rats inside removed.

question: Are rats in the attic dangerous?

children.text: They can be. Florida DOH links chewed wiring to fires, and the CDC links rodent droppings and urine to disease. Don't sweep or vacuum droppings, and keep children out of the attic.

question: Can rats get from the attic into the house?

children.text: Yes. UF/IFAS says rats climb wires, pipes and rough walls, squeeze through cracks half an inch wide, and can even come up through toilets. A rat seen indoors means the attic problem has spread.

question: Is it safe to sleep with rats in the attic?

children.text: The main risks are chewed wiring, droppings and, less often, bites; UF/IFAS notes rats sometimes bite sleeping children. Florida DOH warns chewed wires can start fires, and the CDC links rodent droppings and urine to disease. Get it dealt with soon, and keep the attic hatch closed meanwhile.

question: Can I just put poison in the attic?

children.text: UF/IFAS Extension calls rodenticides a last resort, to be used only in tamper-resistant bait stations. Poison does nothing about the gap the rats use, and more will come.

question: Why did bats pick my attic?

children.text: FWC says bats may roost in buildings that mimic their natural roosts, especially after their natural habitat is disturbed. A warm, dark attic with a small gap at the roofline fits the bill.

question: Can I seal the hole while the bats are out at night?

children.text: No. Some bats stay in, and in maternity season the pups can't fly. FWC warns that bats that can't get out before the exit is sealed die inside the building.

question: Will the bats leave in winter?

children.text: Plan the exclusion instead of waiting. Book it for the legal window, August 15 to April 15, and make sure overnight lows are forecast at 50°F or warmer so the bats are active and actually leave.

question: Can I get rabies from bats in my attic?

children.text: Only through a bite or scratch, which is why bats shouldn't be handled. FWC's brochure calls rabies in bats rare. Florida's Department of Health still names bats as one of the state's two main wildlife sources of rabies, so any contact with a bat needs a call to your county health department.

question: Can bats get from the attic into my living space?

children.text: Sometimes a single bat does. FWC notes that a maternity colony is usually not found in rooms where people live or work, because the mothers need a warm, undisturbed roost. Repeated bats indoors point to a gap between the attic and the house.

question: Do I need to replace the insulation?

children.text: Usually only under the roost, where guano has built up. It depends on how long the bats were there.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: how you decide how much insulation to replace after bats]

question: Are bats in the attic a health risk?

children.text: Mostly through guano dust and bat bites. Don't go into a guano-covered attic without a respirator, and don't handle bats with bare hands.

question: How many species of bats are in Florida?

children.text: FWC's brochure counts 13 resident species, and all of them eat night-flying insects. The Brazilian free-tailed bat is one FWC calls common in Florida buildings.

question: Why is a raccoon in my attic?

children.text: UF/IFAS says raccoons usually den in hollow trees, and where cavities are scarce they use attics and crawl spaces. They get in where an entry point hasn't been kept up or repaired.

question: Will the raccoon leave on its own?

children.text: Sometimes, but a mother with kits stays until they're older, and UF/IFAS notes a raccoon often comes back to a den it knows. Get it out properly and close the way in.

question: Can I scare it out?

children.text: UF/IFAS describes one-way devices for raccoons without young, and for a mother with kits, putting cloth soaked in male raccoon or predator urine near the den so she moves them. These need the family out before anything is sealed. If you're unsure, call us.

question: The mother is gone and the babies are still up there. What now?

children.text: Don't seal anything, and don't handle the kits yourself. Call us. Young left alone in an attic need to be found and taken care of quickly and carefully.

question: Can I clean up the raccoon droppings myself?

children.text: In a yard, FWC and the CDC advise gloves, prompt removal, and burning or burying the droppings or bagging them for the landfill, then washing your hands. In an attic, with insulation and tight spaces, it's safer to have it done.

question: How do I keep raccoons out of the attic?

children.text: Get the entry sealed with strong materials, cap the chimney and keep branches off the roof. Don't put out food or garbage in a way that draws them: Florida rule 68A-4.001 bans doing that when it creates a nuisance. See
raccoon removal

question: Is a raccoon in the attic dangerous?

children.text: Raccoons usually avoid people, but they bite when cornered, and Florida's Department of Health names raccoons as a main wildlife source of rabies. Don't go up into the attic to look for it.

question: Why do squirrels get into attics?

children.text: For a dry, protected nest site close to food. FWC says squirrels occur in woodlands and urban areas, especially near pines, oaks and hickories, and sometimes nest in attics when they can get in.

question: When do squirrels have babies in Florida?

children.text: FWC says Florida squirrels tend to breed twice a year, producing litters in spring and autumn. Those are the months to check for young before closing anything.

question: Will squirrels leave the attic on their own?

children.text: They leave every day to feed, then come back. Closing the hole while they're out, without checking for young first, can trap a litter inside.

question: Can squirrels chew through wiring?

children.text: Yes. FWC names chewing on everything from plants to vehicle wires as a common squirrel complaint, and suggests covering wires and PVC pipe where squirrels can reach them. If you see bare wire in the attic, have it checked. See
squirrels chewing wires

question: Do squirrels carry diseases?

children.text: The CDC lists squirrels among the rodents that can spread rat-bite fever through bites, scratches, or contact with saliva or urine. Don't handle squirrels or their nests bare-handed.

question: How do I keep squirrels off my roof?

children.text: Trim branches well back from the roof, as FWC recommends, and close damaged soffits, vents, loose tiles and gaps where the roof meets the wall.

question: Can I trap the squirrel myself?

children.text: Florida allows cage traps for nuisance gray and flying squirrels, checked at least once every 24 hours. A trapped squirrel can only be released on site, on 40 acres or more in the same county with written permission, or humanely put down. Fox squirrels can't be hunted, and the threatened Big Cypress fox squirrel can't be trapped without a permit. See the rules above.

question: What if the squirrel is inside the house, not the attic?

children.text: FWC's advice: move pets to another room and open an outside door or window so the squirrel can find its own way out.

question: Why would an opossum be in my attic?

children.text: Shelter. UF/IFAS says opossums don't dig their own burrows. They use hollow logs, woodpiles, barns, abandoned buildings and other animals' burrows, so a gap into a quiet attic or crawl space works too.

question: I saw the opossum in daylight. Is it rabid?

children.text: Probably not. FWC says opossums are mostly nocturnal but may be active in the day, which is normal and not by itself a sign of illness. Rabies is also rare in opossums: UF/IFAS calls them nearly immune.

question: Is it a mother with babies?

children.text: Possibly, especially from February to June. FWC says the young ride in the pouch, then on the mother's back from about 80 days, so they usually move with her.

question: Will an opossum hurt my dog or cat?

children.text: Opossums try to bluff first. FWC says they hiss, drool and growl, and may play dead if the threat continues. Keep pets away from the den and don't let them corner it.

question: Do opossums eat rats?

children.text: They might. UF/IFAS describes opossums as opportunistic omnivores that eat insects, frogs, snakes, small mammals and carrion, along with fruit and garbage. An opossum isn't a fix for a rat problem, though: for that, see
rat removal

question: How do I keep opossums out of my attic and crawl space?

children.text: Once you're sure none are inside, repair screens and block vents and gaps with sturdy wire mesh, as FWC recommends. Bring pet food in at night and secure trash and fallen fruit.

question: Do opossums do any good?

children.text: Yes. FWC says they eat dead animals much like a vulture, eat ticks they find while grooming, and are at least partly immune to snake venom, so they'll eat venomous snakes. Just not in your attic.

rats in the attic

question: Who do I call about injured wildlife in St. Pete?

question: Am I responsible for rats on my St. Petersburg property?

children.text: Yes. St. Petersburg's code requires owners or occupants to eliminate rodent infestations, and occupants of single-family and two-family homes are responsible for their own pest control.

). Avoid physical contact with wild animals such as raccoons and bats.

question: Can I feed the raccoons in my Sarasota yard?

children.text: No. FWC rule 68A-4.001 bars placing food in a manner that attracts raccoons (
FWC

what to do about raccoons

children.text: Don't keep it. UF/IFAS Extension in Sarasota County says holding sick or injured wildlife longer than it takes to get it to a licensed rehabilitator violates Florida law, and it points to the Wildlife Center of Southwest Florida, 941-484-9657 (
UF/IFAS

question: Do I need an exterminator for rats in my Sarasota rental?

WWSB

raccoons in the attic

dead animal removal

opossum removal

sections.heading: Who we are and how it works

children.text: Pro Wildlife Removal removes bats, rats, raccoons, squirrels, snakes, opossums (possums), armadillos, bees and dead animals from homes and businesses in eight counties across Central Florida. We inspect, remove the animals the way Florida law allows and seal the entry points. Call (844) 264-6254.
Pick the critter you think you have. Each page covers the signs, the Florida rules for that animal and how we get it out.
After the initial inspection, our Pro Wildlife specialist will identify which animals are creating the problem and implement a solution tailored to your specific animal issue.

The trapping and removal process begins with setting up specialized traps to securely capture the animals without causing harm. Once the animals are safely contained, they are promptly removed from the property, ensuring the area is free from wildlife intrusions.

Part of removing an animal from inside or under a structure like a home or an office is to make sure there are no available openings for the animals to come and go freely. Closing these entry points is a key step in making sure that once your animal is out, another one does not move in.

Animals that live in a crawlspace or attic leave droppings, soiled insulation and chewed wiring behind. We show you what the inspection found, so you know what an electrician or contractor may need to look at.
One number covers all eight counties, from Tarpon Springs on the Gulf coast to Ocala and Winter Haven inland: (844) 264-6254.

children.text: Wildlife work in Florida comes with rules: when bats can be excluded, how often traps must be checked, where a trapped animal may be released. We follow them on every job, and we explain them to you, so you know why a job is done the way it is.

Josh Holmberg started Pro Wildlife Removal in 2016. children.text: Florida wildlife keeps a calendar. Knowing it helps you act at the right time, and explains why some jobs have to wait.

cards.title: Bats: April 16 to August 14 is maternity season

children.text: This is when most of Florida's bats give birth and raise their pups, and exclusion isn't allowed in that window without an FWC permit. April 15 is the last day to exclude bats without one, and exclusion can start again August 15. If you hear bats in summer, call anyway: we can inspect and plan the work for the first legal date. Read the
bat maternity season guide

cards.title: Raccoons: babies in March and April

children.text: Most raccoons in Florida are born in March and April, and an attic is a warm, dry den. Thumping and chattering overhead in spring often means a mother with young. They need to be removed together, never sealed in. See
raccoon mating season in Florida

Roof rats are climbers that live high in trees and in the upper levels of homes. Florida DOH says a roof rat can have up to 8 litters a year, so they can turn up in any month. Branches touching the roof are their bridge in, so keep limbs trimmed back. See
signs of rats in the attic
Storm damage to soffits, vents and roof edges leaves openings an animal can use. Get it repaired promptly, and look along the roofline for new gaps after a blow. See
common wildlife entry points

title: Bat Removal
summary: Legal bat exclusion with one-way doors and every entry point sealed, outside Florida's maternity season.

cardImage.alt: Bat hanging upside down with its wings folded

hero.heading: Bat Removal in Central Florida

children.text: Bats in the attic, soffit or tile roof, moved out the legal way: one-way doors, then every gap sealed.

image.alt: Bat hanging upside down with its wings folded

sections.heading: How do you get bats out of a house in Florida?

children.text: In Florida, bats are removed by exclusion: one-way devices on the exits let the bats fly out at night and stop them coming back, then the openings are sealed. It's legal from August 15 to April 15. Killing, trapping or poisoning bats is illegal. Call (844) 264-6254 for an inspection.
A colony can live in a roof for months before anyone notices. These are the clues, roughly in the order people spot them. More on
bats in the attic
Stand outside at sunset and watch the roofline. Bats dropping out of the same gap in a soffit, gable vent or roof tile, one after another, is the clearest sign of a roost.
Bat droppings, called guano, are black and dry. They pile up under the roost and below the openings bats use: on a lanai floor, a windowsill, a pool cage frame or the attic insulation.
Bats use the same crack night after night, and the oils and dirt from their fur leave a light brown stain around it.
Bats leave the roost around dusk and come back around dawn. That's when you're likely to hear light scratching or chirping in a wall or ceiling.

An established roost builds up droppings and urine, and the smell can reach the rooms below. FWC calls it a quality-of-life problem rather than a health hazard, but it doesn't go away until the guano does.
One bat in a bedroom may have come in through an open door. Two or more, or one that keeps coming back, points to a roost in the walls or attic.

sections.heading: Bats are useful outdoors. Inside your walls, they're a problem.

children.text: Florida has 13 resident bat species, and all of them eat night-flying insects. The state protects them for good reason. The trouble starts when a colony moves into a building. Here is what the health agencies actually say, without the scare talk.
Rabies.

Florida's Department of Health names raccoons and bats as the main wildlife sources of rabies in the state. Not all bats carry rabies, but the CDC warns that bat bites can be so small you may not know you were bitten.
Histoplasmosis.

This lung infection comes from a fungus that grows in soil mixed with bird and bat droppings, and people catch it by breathing in the spores. FWC notes that no case from bat guano in a building has been reported in Florida, and the CDC still recommends a respirator in a confined space with guano.
The house itself.
Bats don't chew or tear up a building the way rats and raccoons do. The damage is the guano piling up on the insulation, the stains and the smell.
If you wake up with a bat in the room, or find one near a child or a pet, don't let it go. The CDC says to call your county health department or animal control first so the bat can be tested.
Bats can't be trapped and carried off like a raccoon. The colony has to leave on its own and find the door locked behind it. Here is how that works on your house.

We inspect the whole outside of the building, not just the gap you saw bats use: the roofline, soffits, vents, flashing and tile. Bats only need a small gap. Miss one, and the colony just moves to it.

If it's between April 16 and August 14, the pups may not be able to fly yet. We don't exclude in that window. We document the roost, close the openings bats aren't using, and book the exclusion for August 15 or after.

Tubes or netting go on the active exits. Bats leave at dusk to feed and can't get back in. FWC requires the devices to stay up at least four nights, with overnight lows forecast at 50°F or warmer, so the bats are active and actually leave.
Once the last bat is out, the devices come down and every opening is sealed. We point out any guano and soiled insulation we saw, so you can plan what happens next.

sections.heading: Florida's bat rules, in plain words

children.text: Bats can't be killed.
It's illegal under Florida Administrative Code rule 68A-4.001.
No poison, no pesticides, no fumigants.
Rule 68A-9.010 bans pesticides and poisons used to harm, kill or drive off bats, and FWC says fumigants are illegal on bats too.
No trapping or relocating.
FWC says capturing and moving bats is illegal and doesn't work anyway.
No exclusion in maternity season without a permit.
April 16 to August 14 is when most Florida bats give birth and raise their young. April 15 is the last legal day without a permit, and exclusion opens again on August 15.
Exclusion has to be done right.
Devices on the key exits, left up at least four nights, with overnight lows forecast at 50°F or above.
Don't seal bats in.
A bat that can't get out dies inside the wall or attic, and then you have a smell and a second problem.
Read FWC's own page on
bats in buildings
, or our
homeowner's guide to Florida bat laws
and
bat maternity season guide

sections.heading: After the bats are out
checklist: Every opening bats used, and the gaps next to them, sealed with materials that hold up to Florida weather
Barrel tile, ridge vents and soffit returns closed where bats can slip under
Guano and soiled insulation pointed out, so you know what the bats left
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: is there a warranty on bat exclusion work, and how long?]

children.text: Getting the colony out is half the job. The other half is making sure it can't come back. How much guano is left depends on how long the bats lived there: a few weeks leaves a little on top of the insulation, years can soak it through.

image.alt: Bat hanging upside down with its wings folded

children.text: A single-story ranch is quicker than a two-story house with a steep tile roof.

cards.title: How long the colony has been there

children.text: A new roost leaves little behind. An old one can mean removing the insulation under it.
Rotted fascia, broken soffit panels or cracked tile have to be repaired first, by a contractor the owner arranges.

title: Rat Removal
summary: Roof rats out of the attic: every entry point sealed and the rats left inside trapped.

cardImage.alt: Rat caught in a live trap

hero.heading: Rat Removal in Central Florida

children.text: Scratching in the ceiling at night? We find how the rats get in, close every gap and trap the ones still inside.

image.alt: Rat caught in a live trap

sections.heading: How do you get rid of rats in the attic in Florida?

children.text: Seal every gap a rat can use, then trap the rats left inside. Traps alone don't work while the openings stay open, because new rats keep coming in. In Florida it's usually roof rats, which climb trees and wires to reach the roof. Call (844) 264-6254 for an inspection.
Rats are active mostly at night, so many people never see one. They see what the rats leave behind. More on
rats in the attic
Scratching, gnawing and scurrying in the ceiling or walls after dark. Squeaking from one spot can mean a nest of young.
Roof rat droppings are up to half an inch long and pointed at the ends. Fresh ones are black and shiny. Old ones turn gray and crumble. Look in the attic, along walls and in the back of cabinets.
Rats use the same paths again and again, and the oil in their fur leaves dark, greasy rub marks on walls, beams, pipes and wires and around the holes they use.
Fresh gnawing on wood is light-colored with sharp, splintery edges. Check attic wiring, the edges of beams, soffit vents and A/C line covers.
Florida DOH says roof rats are known for hollowing out citrus fruit in trees or on the ground. Gnawed oranges on the tree or under it mean rats nearby, often with a short trip to your roof.

Norway rats dig. Florida DOH says they burrow under buildings and beneath concrete slabs. UF/IFAS describes burrow openings of about 3 inches, with fresh dirt scattered in front and worn runways leading in.

sections.heading: Why rats in the attic can't wait

children.text: A few rats become a lot of rats fast. Florida DOH says roof rats can have up to 8 litters a year, each with 6 to 8 young, and the young become sexually active 2 to 3 months after birth.
Fire risk.
A rat's front teeth never stop growing, so it gnaws to keep them short. Florida DOH notes rats can cause fires by chewing through the insulation on electrical wires.
Disease.

The CDC says rodents spread disease through their droppings, urine, saliva and bites. Rat-bite fever spreads through bites, scratches, or contact with a rodent's saliva or urine, and it needs fast treatment.
Damage.
Gnawed rafters and wiring, nests in the insulation, and droppings and urine spread through it.
UF/IFAS says rodent-proofing must block all possible entry points to work. It lists sealing as the first step and trapping as the last. That's the order we follow.

A rat fits through a crack half an inch wide. We check the roofline, gable and soffit vents, roof returns, plumbing stacks, A/C line openings, garage door corners and where pipes enter the walls, and we look for the branches and wires the rats use to reach the roof.
Openings are closed with rodent-resistant materials: sheet metal, hardware cloth with quarter-inch mesh, mortar or concrete. Spray foam isn't on that list.
With the doors closed, the rats left in the attic are trapped where they travel. Traps are checked on a schedule until the activity stops.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: what traps you use and how often a technician comes back to check them]
Rats test new seals in the first couple of weeks, so the work is checked and any break is fixed.

sections.heading: What Florida's rules mean for rats

children.text: Rats can't be released.
Roof rats and Norway rats aren't native to Florida, and FWC says non-native wildlife may not be relocated or released. A rat caught alive can't be let go somewhere else.
Poison is a last resort.
UF/IFAS Extension says rodenticides should only be used in tamper-resistant bait stations, away from children and pets, and only EPA-registered products.
Skip the glue boards.
UF/IFAS calls glue traps inhumane, and the CDC says glue and live traps can scare rodents into urinating, which raises the risk of illness.
That's why we lean on sealing rather than poison. More in
rat exclusion and preventing reinfestation

sections.heading: Rat droppings: what the CDC says
checklist: Droppings, nests and soiled insulation shown to you in the inspection
Chewed wiring pointed out so an electrician can check it
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: is there a warranty on rat exclusion work, and how long?]

children.text: Rat droppings and urine can carry germs, and sweeping or vacuuming them puts dust in the air. The CDC's advice is to wet droppings with a disinfectant or a bleach solution first, wait five minutes, then pick them up with paper towels. In an attic with years of droppings through the insulation, that is work for protective gear and respirators.

children.text: We price rat jobs after the inspection, once we know how many openings there are and how hard they are to reach. See
what drives wildlife removal costs
for more.
The rat inspection is free. We walk the roofline and attic, then give you the price before any work starts.
A tile roof with many gaps takes more sealing than a shingle roof with one bad vent.

title: Raccoon Removal
summary: Raccoons out of the attic, soffit or crawl space, mothers and young kept together, then the entry sealed.

hero.heading: Raccoon Removal in Central Florida

children.text: Thumping in the attic or a torn soffit? We get the raccoons out, babies included, and seal the way in.

image.alt: Close-up of a raccoon's face

sections.heading: How do you get a raccoon out of the attic in Florida?

children.text: Find out whether there are babies, remove the raccoons by live trap, one-way door or by hand, keeping mother and young together, then seal the entry. In spring, assume a mother with kits. A trapped raccoon may only be released on site or on 40+ contiguous acres in the same county with written permission. Call (844) 264-6254.
Raccoons are big, strong and not subtle. If one is living in your house, you'll usually know. More on
raccoons in the attic
Raccoons are far heavier than rats, and it shows: slow, heavy steps and thumps rather than a light scurry. In spring, listen for the calls of kits too.

cards.title: A torn soffit or roof vent

children.text: UF/IFAS says raccoons get into attics where an entry point isn't maintained or repaired. A rotted or loose soffit, a damaged roof vent or a gap at the roof edge with bent or torn material around it is a strong clue.
UF/IFAS lists open chimneys among the common ways raccoons get into a house. Scratching and calling from the fireplace in spring often means a den with young.

cards.title: A pile of droppings in one spot

children.text: Raccoons share toilet spots called latrines. FWC says in suburbs they turn up under trees, in sandboxes and on decks and patios. Droppings piled together in one place point to raccoons.
Knocked-over garbage cans and empty pet bowls in the morning mean raccoons are feeding nearby, and a den is often close.
UF/IFAS notes raccoons also move in under mobile homes and decks. Look for gaps in the skirting and lattice.

sections.heading: Why raccoons in the house need to go

children.text: Raccoons aren't out to hurt anyone, but an attic den brings real problems.
Rabies.

Along with bats, raccoons are one of the two main wildlife carriers of rabies in Florida, according to the state Department of Health. UF/IFAS puts the share of wild raccoons exposed to rabies at fewer than 1 in 200: low, but not a risk to ignore. Never corner or handle one.
Raccoon roundworm.

The CDC says people can be infected by swallowing the parasite's eggs from raccoon droppings, usually by accident, and that most cases are in children. FWC says the roundworm appears widespread in Florida but at low levels. Infections are rare and can be severe.
Damage.
Torn soffits, vents and roof edges, crushed and soiled insulation, and rain getting in through the hole they made.
Most raccoons in Florida are born in March and April, according to UF/IFAS. From late winter into summer, the first question on any raccoon job is: are there babies?

We find the entry hole, any other weak spots, and the den. If there are young, we locate them before anything else happens. Wildlife agencies warn against sealing an entry while young are inside, because they'd be cut off from their mother.

Depending on the house and the season, the adult is caught in a live trap checked at least every 24 hours, or leaves through a one-way door. Kits are taken out by hand so mother and young stay together.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: confirm how you handle a mother with kits (reuniting, use of a heated box, etc.)]

Florida allows three outcomes for a trapped raccoon: release on the property where it was caught, release on at least 40 contiguous acres in the same county with the landowner's written permission, or humane euthanasia. FWC's roundworm guidance also says not to relocate raccoons.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: what you do with trapped raccoons (release on site, release on permitted land, or euthanasia)]
The entry hole is sealed with materials a raccoon can't pull apart, and other weak spots are closed. We show you any latrine or soiled insulation we found.

sections.heading: Florida's raccoon rules, in plain words

children.text: A trap can't sit for days.
Florida requires every trap to be inspected at least once every 24 hours, and an animal caught alive has to be released legally or humanely put down within 24 hours of capture or inspection.
Three legal outcomes, and only three.

Under Florida's nuisance wildlife rule (68A-9.010), a trapped raccoon may be released on the same property, released on at least 40 contiguous acres in the same county with the landowner's written permission, or humanely put down.
No park drop-offs.
Letting a raccoon go in a park, or on any land without the owner's written permission, is illegal. FWC's roundworm page goes further and says not to relocate raccoons at all.
New FWC trapping rules start December 31, 2026.
They change trap check times, allow remote (camera) checks, and require most people who trap to complete FWC's annual registration and training, which FWC says is
at no cost

. A homeowner using one regular-size cage trap (door up to 20 by 28 inches) on their own property, to catch nuisance or non-native wildlife, doesn't need registration, training or reporting. Nuisance animals moved off site must be released or put down within 12 hours of the trap check, down from 24. Details at
MyFWC.com/TrappingRules
Don't feed them.
Florida rule 68A-4.001 bans putting out food or garbage in a way that attracts raccoons and creates, or is likely to create, a public nuisance. Pet food left out at night draws raccoons in.

image.alt: Close-up of a gray squirrel eating

sections.heading: How do you get squirrels out of the attic in Florida?

children.text: Check for a nest of young first, then get the squirrels out with a one-way door or cage traps, and seal every gap along the roofline. Florida squirrels have litters in spring and autumn. A trapped squirrel can only be released on site or on approved land in the same county. Call (844) 264-6254.
Squirrels keep daylight hours, which is the easiest way to tell them from rats in the attic. More on
squirrels in the attic

cards.title: Noise in the morning and afternoon

children.text: Gray squirrels keep daylight hours, so running and scratching overhead during the day points to them. Noise after dark points to rats, or to flying squirrels, which come out at night.

cards.title: A chewed hole at the roofline

children.text: A gnawed opening in a soffit, fascia board or roof edge, with fresh, light-colored wood showing around it.
Squirrels running along the roof, or jumping onto it from an oak or a branch that hangs over the house, and then disappearing at the same spot.
FWC notes gray squirrels sometimes nest in attics when they can get in. Look for leaves and shredded material piled in the eaves or the insulation.
Florida squirrels tend to have their young in spring and autumn. Steady activity from one spot in those months can mean a litter.
FWC says squirrels' front teeth never stop growing, so they chew constantly. Wires and PVC in the attic, and in parked cars, are common targets.

sections.heading: Why squirrels in the attic are more than a noise

children.text: A squirrel has to chew. FWC explains that its front teeth grow constantly and chewing keeps them filed down. Outside, that's bark and nuts. Inside your attic, it's whatever is there.
Wiring and pipes.
FWC says chewing damage, from plants to vehicle wires, is a common squirrel complaint, and suggests covering PVC and electrical wires where squirrels can reach them.
The roof.
A chewed opening lets in rain, and it's a ready-made door for the next animal.
More squirrels.
FWC says Florida squirrels tend to breed twice a year, with litters averaging one to four young. A pair in the attic in winter can be a family by spring.

image.alt: Close-up of a gray squirrel eating

children.text: Remove, seal, check: done in that order, after a careful look for babies.

We find the main hole and every weak spot, using FWC's list of common squirrel entries: damaged soffits, broken screens, roof tiles, gaps where the roof meets the wall, and attic vents. In spring and autumn, we look for a litter before anything is closed.
Usually a one-way door on the main hole lets the squirrels leave and not return. Where that won't work, cage traps are set and checked at least every 24 hours.

Fox squirrels are different.

title: Snake Removal
summary: A snake in the house, garage or pool cage removed safely, the way in found and closed, and the rodents that drew it dealt with.

hero.heading: Snake Removal in Central Florida

children.text: A snake in the house, garage or lanai? Keep your distance and call. We remove it safely, find how it got in and close the gap.

image.alt: Close-up of a patterned python

sections.heading: What should I do about a snake in my house in Florida?

children.text: Keep children and pets away, watch where it goes from a safe distance, and don't try to catch or kill it. Only 6 of Florida's 50 snake species are venomous, but a bite from any snake hurts. Call (844) 264-6254 and we'll remove it and close the way in.

sections.heading: The venomous snakes you may meet in Central Florida

children.text: FWC's guide to Florida's venomous snakes lists six species. Three are found in every Florida county, and the coral snake lives throughout the state. Learn them, then leave identification of any snake you're unsure about to us.

The other two, the timber (canebrake) rattlesnake and the copperhead, are north Florida snakes. FWC's guide places the canebrake mainly in northern Florida and the copperhead in a few northwest counties.
Yellow-bordered diamonds down the back, a rattle and a head much wider than the neck. A large, venomous native snake, found in every county, often in palmetto flatlands, pine woods and brushy fields.
Small, stout and gray, also called the ground rattler. Its tiny rattle sounds like a buzzing insect and can only be heard a few feet away. Common in every county.
A heavy-bodied pit viper with no rattle, olive-brown to black, usually around three feet long. Lives near water: stream banks, swamps, lake edges and marshes. Found in every county.

Red, yellow and black rings with a black nose. On a coral snake the red rings touch the yellow; on the harmless scarlet kingsnake, red touches black. Found throughout Florida in leaf litter, logs and brush piles.

sections.heading: Why snakes come to your house

children.text: Snakes go where the food is. FWC says seeing snakes often around a house or shed may mean rodents are there, and UF/IFAS notes that rat snakes move into attics, garages and sheds when rodents are present and leave once the rodents are gone.
Rodents.
Rats in the attic or mice in the garage are a dinner bell. If you keep finding snakes, the real job may be
rat removal
Cover.
Brush piles, stacked lumber, firewood on the ground, overgrown shrubs and clutter give snakes places to hide.
Water and frogs.
A backyard pond full of frogs draws the snakes that eat them.
Easy ways in.
UF/IFAS warns some snakes can fit through an opening no bigger than a pencil: gaps under doors, worn garage door seals, pet doors, holes around pipes and open pool-cage drain pipes.
Most snakes around Florida homes are harmless and eat pests. FWC's advice is to leave a snake outdoors alone. The problem is one inside the house, the garage or the pool cage.

image.alt: Close-up of a patterned python

children.text: Where the snake is, how big it looks, its colors, and whether it's still in sight. If you can, take a photo from a safe distance. Keep the door to that room closed.
The technician identifies the snake and removes it with tools made for the job.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: describe how you capture snakes, venomous and not]
Native snakes are released where Florida rules allow. Protected species, like the eastern indigo snake, are left unharmed.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: where you release snakes, and how you handle venomous ones]
We look for the gap the snake used, and for what drew it: rodents, a pond or cover next to the house. Then we close the gaps and tell you what else to change.
Some snakes are protected.

The eastern indigo snake, a bluish-black, non-venomous snake that can reach eight feet, is a threatened species under the federal Endangered Species Act and Florida rule 68A-27. It shows no aggression when approached. Leave it be.
Killing a snake is rarely justified.
FWC says there's no good reason to kill a snake except in the unlikely case of a venomous snake posing immediate danger to people or pets. Snakes usually bite only when they're handled or provoked.
Keeping a venomous snake needs state approval.
FWC says venomous reptiles may only be possessed with its authorization, so catching one to keep or move is not a do-it-yourself job.
Snake repellents don't work.
UF/IFAS says plainly that the products sold as snake repellents simply do not work.

children.text: An opossum (possum) living under the house, in the crawl space or in the attic? We remove it humanely, young included, and close the way in.

image.alt: Opossum on a wooden fence

sections.heading: How do I get rid of an opossum under my house in Florida?

children.text: Remove what draws it (pet food, trash, fallen fruit), make sure the opossum is out, then close the opening with wire mesh. If it won't leave, it can be live-trapped and released only on site or on approved land in the same county. Removing one doesn't stop the next. Call (844) 264-6254.
Opossums are mostly out at night, so the signs usually show up by morning. More on
opossums in the attic

cards.title: A gray, cat-sized animal at night

children.text: Pale to dark gray fur, a pointed snout, small bare ears and a long, hairless tail. FWC notes it's normal to see one in daylight too, and not necessarily a sign it's sick.

cards.title: A gap under the house or deck

children.text: Torn skirting, a pushed-in foundation vent, or a hole under a shed, porch or A/C pad with a worn path leading to it.
Opossums eat almost anything. Tipped trash, empty pet bowls left outside and dropped fruit gone overnight are classic signs.
Shuffling or thumping under the floor or in the crawl space at night, when an opossum comes and goes.
FWC notes a threatened opossum may play dead and give off a foul smell. Pets that corner one under the house often bring the smell back with them.
FWC lists sleeping chickens and their eggs among the things opossums take at night.

sections.heading: Opossums are helpful, just not under your floor

children.text: Opossums do useful work. FWC says they clean up dead animals much like a vulture, eat ticks they find while grooming, and can even eat venomous snakes because they're at least partly immune to the venom. UF/IFAS describes them as nearly immune to rabies. Living under your home is still a problem:
Mess and smell.
Droppings, urine and nesting material build up under the floor or in the insulation.
Damage.
Torn screens and vents where they push their way in.
Pets and chickens.
A cornered opossum hisses, growls and may bite. FWC also notes opossums take chickens and eggs at night.
Horses.
FWC says opossums are one of the main sources of the parasite that causes EPM in horses. Barn owners should cover feed and keep wildlife out of hay storage.

image.alt: Opossum on a wooden fence

children.text: Opossums in Florida have their young mostly from February to June, and a mother carries them in her pouch, then on her back. The plan has to account for the babies.

cards.title: Find the den and the openings

children.text: We locate where the opossum sleeps and every gap it uses, under the house, deck, shed or in the attic, and check for a mother with young.

Often the simplest way is to wait until the opossum leaves for the night and then block the opening. Where it won't leave, it's caught in a live trap checked at least every 24 hours. A mother with young is removed with her babies.

Once we're sure every opossum is out, torn screens, vents and gaps are blocked with wire mesh, as FWC recommends.
Opossums are native and can be removed as nuisance animals
when they cause or are about to cause damage, threaten public safety, or cause a problem in, under or on a building (rule 68A-9.010).

MyFWC.com/TrappingRules
Steel traps need an FWC permit,
and shooting one at night needs a Gun and Light at Night Permit. Leave both to professionals.

image.alt: Two armadillos caught in a cage trap

sections.heading: How do I get rid of an armadillo in my yard in Florida?

children.text: Trap it at its active burrow, then make the yard less inviting. Poison baits are illegal, and no repellents or fumigants are registered for armadillos in Florida. A trapped armadillo must be released on site, on 40 or more contiguous acres in the same county with the landowner's written permission, or humanely put down. Call (844) 264-6254.
Armadillos are mostly out at night, digging for insects and grubs with their noses and strong claws. What you find in the morning tells the story.

cards.title: Small holes all over the lawn

children.text: Shallow holes about 1 to 3 inches deep and 3 to 5 inches wide, where an armadillo rooted for grubs and worms overnight.
An entrance up to about a foot across, sometimes dug right under a driveway, patio or other structure. FWC says one armadillo can keep several burrows with more than one entrance.
Mulch thrown out of the beds and plants uprooted. FWC notes moist, fertilized soil draws the earthworms and larvae armadillos hunt.

cards.title: An armadillo at dusk or after dark

children.text: An armored animal about 15 to 17 inches long, not counting the tail, nosing along the ground. Armadillos see poorly, so they may not notice you.

cards.title: Digging where the soil stays wet

children.text: Fresh holes in wet, heavily watered parts of the yard, where worms and larvae come up near the surface.
UF/IFAS warns that armadillo burrows under driveways and patios can cause structural damage. A slab that starts to crack or sink near a burrow needs a look.

sections.heading: Why an armadillo by the house is worth dealing with

children.text: FWC calls armadillos helpful in one way: they eat large numbers of grubs, spiders, cockroaches and other insects. The trouble is where they dig. UF/IFAS says a single armadillo keeps an average of ten burrows, each up to 7 feet deep and 20 feet long.
Your slab and driveway.
A burrow under a driveway or patio can undermine it, according to UF/IFAS.
The lawn and beds.
Night after night of rooting can wreck sod and landscaping.
Disease, handled with care.

The CDC says some armadillos naturally carry the bacteria that cause leprosy (Hansen's disease), but the risk is very low and most people who come into contact with them are unlikely to get leprosy. As a simple precaution, wear gloves and don't handle armadillos bare-handed.

image.alt: Two armadillos caught in a cage trap

children.text: Armadillos are hard to bait. UF/IFAS research found they only notice food at very close range, and that where a trap sits matters more than what's in it.
We look for fresh digging and tracks to find the burrow the armadillo is using now, and its travel routes along fences and walls.

[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: do you install exclusion fencing or wire along foundations?]
Armadillos are treated as native in Florida.
FWC considers them naturalized: they spread here from the southwest. That means they're covered by the nuisance wildlife rule, 68A-9.010.

Release only on site, or on 40+ contiguous acres in the same county with written permission.

No poison, no repellents.

New FWC trapping rules start December 31, 2026.
They change trap check times, allow remote (camera) checks, and require most people who trap to complete FWC's annual registration and training, which FWC says is
at no cost

. A homeowner using one regular-size cage trap (door up to 20 by 28 inches) on their own property, to catch nuisance or non-native wildlife, doesn't need registration, training or reporting. Nuisance animals moved off site must be released or put down within 12 hours of the trap check, down from 24. Details at
MyFWC.com/TrappingRules

title: Bee Removal
summary: Honey bees in a wall, soffit, shed or meter box: what Florida law allows, why the comb matters, and what to do until help arrives.

cardImage.alt: Honey bee swarm clustered on a deck railing

hero.heading: Bee Removal in Central Florida

children.text: Bees going in and out of a wall, soffit or shed? Keep people and pets back, leave the opening alone, and call.

image.alt: Honey bee swarm clustered on a deck railing

sections.heading: What should I do about bees in my wall in Florida?

children.text: Don't spray them and don't seal the hole: blocking it drives the bees deeper into the house. In Florida, a colony should be removed alive by a registered beekeeper or eradicated by a licensed pest control operator, and the comb taken out. Keep people and pets away and call (844) 264-6254.

sections.heading: The bees you're likely to find at home

children.text: Not every bee around the house is a problem, and each kind nests differently. Look from a safe distance before you do anything.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: which stinging insects you handle (honey bees, carpenter bees, bumble bees, wasps or yellow jackets)]
Live in large colonies inside cavities: walls, soffits, sheds, water meters. In Central Florida these can be European, African or a mix, and a colony in a structure needs a professional.
Look like bumble bees but have a shiny, greenish-black abdomen. UF/IFAS says they drill clean, half-inch holes into trim, railings and siding and tunnel 3 to 6 inches into the wood.
Fuzzy all over. UF/IFAS says Florida's five species nest at or below ground, often in old rodent burrows, dense grass or crevices by a foundation, and the colony dies off by early winter.

sections.heading: Swarm or colony? How to tell

children.text: UF/IFAS draws a clear line between the two, and it changes what needs to happen.

cards.title: A swarm: a ball of bees in the open

children.text: A cluster hanging on a branch, fence or eave. UF/IFAS says swarms are temporary, staying a few hours to a few days, and are usually calm because they have no nest to defend.

cards.title: A colony: bees flying in and out of a hole

children.text: A steady line of bees going into a gap in a wall, soffit, roof edge or shed. That means comb, honey and young inside, and bees that will defend them.
A buzz you can hear through drywall, or a warm spot on an inside wall, can mean comb behind it.
Dark stains or sticky honey on a wall or ceiling. UF/IFAS notes comb left in a wall can melt into the structure and stain it.
UF/IFAS lists water meters, gutter downspouts, pipes, holes in siding, cinderblocks, under sheds and under playground equipment as common nest sites.
If a cluster in the open is building wax comb, UF/IFAS warns it's the start of a colony, not a passing swarm.

sections.heading: Why Florida bee colonies need care

children.text: Honey bees matter, and a swarm passing through is usually better left alone. A colony living in your house or next to where people walk is different, especially in Central Florida.
African honey bees are here.
UF/IFAS says African bees were first documented in Florida in 2001 near the Port of Tampa and have spread through the southern half of the state, mixing with European honey bees.
They defend hard.
UF/IFAS says an African colony may send out hundreds or thousands of bees in response to a disturbance and chase an intruder 400 yards or more.
Sealing the hole backfires.
UF/IFAS warns that closing an active opening forces bees further into the wall and possibly into the living space.
Comb left behind causes damage.
Honey, wax and dead brood left in a wall can melt, stain, smell and draw wax moths, beetles and other pests, according to UF/IFAS.

image.alt: Honey bee swarm clustered on a deck railing

sections.heading: What to do when you find bees

children.text: Move people and pets away from the area. UF/IFAS says untrained people should never disturb a colony.
Note where the bees go in and out, and whether it's a loose cluster in the open or a steady stream into a hole.
Spraying or blocking the entrance can push the colony deeper into the wall. Leave the opening alone.
Tell us where the bees are, how high, and whether anyone has been stung.

sections.heading: From the first call to a sealed wall

children.text: We find where the bees go in, whether it's a swarm or a colony, and where the comb sits. In a wall, that can mean feeling for warmth and listening for the hum, as UF/IFAS describes.
How the colony will be removed, how the wall or soffit will be opened, and who arranges the repair afterward, all settled before work starts.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: how you handle bees and who does the work; this decides what the page can say]
UF/IFAS says a job isn't finished until the entire nest is out: bees, comb, honey and brood. Leaving it in the wall invites the next problem.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: who removes the colony and comb, and how]
Once the cavity is empty, UF/IFAS advises sealing the opening so a new swarm can't move into the same space.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: do you seal the opening after a bee job?]

sections.heading: Who can remove bees in Florida

children.text: Live removal by a registered beekeeper.

A beekeeper registered with the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) may remove and relocate bees alive without a pest control license (Rule 5E-14.151, F.A.C.). UF/IFAS lists a registered beekeeper or a trained pest control operator for live removal.
Everything else is pest control.
Anyone else removing bees, and anyone killing them, is doing pest control, which needs a licensed pest control company (Chapter 482, Florida Statutes).
The property owner is responsible.
UF/IFAS says dealing with an unwanted swarm or colony is up to the owner of the property.
Neither is required to kill or save.
There's no Florida law that forces either a live removal or an eradication. Colonies that are defensive, near people or animals, or have stung someone may be better eradicated, UF/IFAS says.
The Florida Department of Agriculture keeps a county-by-county Bee Removal or Eradication List. Read UF/IFAS's
Living with the African Honey Bee
and
Nesting Bees and What You Should Do

sections.heading: Keeping the next swarm out
checklist: Gaps of 1/8 inch or more caulked with 100% silicone
Vents, drains, downspouts and plumbing covered with 1/8-inch hardware cloth or insect screen
Water meter covers and holes in siding closed
Old comb removed so it can't melt or draw pests
A weekly look around the house from March to July
Repairs to the wall or soffit are arranged by the owner with a contractor

children.text: UF/IFAS says Florida's swarm season runs from March to July, when swarms are out looking for a cavity with a small opening. These are the fixes it recommends.

summary: A dead animal found and removed from a wall, attic, crawl space or vent, and the way it got in found.

children.text: A smell you can't place, or an animal that died in a wall, attic, crawl space or vent? We find it, remove it and treat the area.

image.alt: Dead raccoon on a roadside

sections.heading: How do you get rid of a dead animal smell in the house?

children.text: Find the animal and remove it. Air fresheners only cover the smell, and in Florida heat it gets worse fast. The source is usually in a wall, attic, crawl space or vent. We locate it, bag and remove it, and find how the animal got in. Call (844) 264-6254.

sections.heading: Signs of a dead animal in your house

children.text: Many people never see the animal. They notice everything around it.

cards.title: A smell that's strongest in one spot

children.text: A sweet, rotten smell that's worse in one room, closet or along one wall, and doesn't go away with cleaning.
Flies gathering at a window, a light or a vent, when doors and windows have been closed.

cards.title: A stain on a wall or ceiling

children.text: A damp or dark spot on drywall or a ceiling below the attic.
Scratching in the attic or walls that went quiet a few days before the smell started.
An odor that comes out when the A/C runs can point to an animal in or near the ductwork.
FWC notes squirrels nest in and chew wiring in cars that sit unused. A smell from the vents or under the hood is worth checking.
[PLACEHOLDER: ask the client: do you remove dead animals from engine bays?]

sections.heading: Why a dead animal shouldn't be left to dry out

children.text: Waiting it out is tempting. In a hot Florida attic or wall, it means weeks of smell and a stained, contaminated spot when it's done.
Health.

The CDC says the risk from animal carcasses is low if proper precautions are taken: gloves, bagging the remains and washing up. In an attic or crawl space, that work comes with insulation, droppings and tight spaces.
Rabies questions.

After a possible exposure, Florida's Department of Health says to contact your county health department or animal control right away. If the animal is dead, don't damage the head and avoid further contact: it may be tested for rabies.
A sign of a bigger problem.
An animal that died inside got in somewhere. Where there was one rat or squirrel, there may be others, and the gap is still open.

image.alt: Dead raccoon on a roadside

children.text: We trace the odor, flies and stains to the spot, then check the attic, crawl space, walls and vents near it.
Gloved, bagged and sealed, following the CDC's handling steps. If it's inside a finished wall, we make the smallest opening that gets it out, and tell you before cutting.
We don't patch drywall: the owner arranges that repair with a contractor.
We show you where the animal was and any soiled insulation around it, so you know what a contractor may need to replace.
We look for how the animal got inside, so you're not doing this again next month. If it's a rat, squirrel or bat problem, we tell you and quote the fix.

sections.heading: If you find a dead animal in the open

children.text: The CDC's own advice is simple: don't touch dead animals with bare hands, and call animal control to remove them. If you do have to move a small animal in the yard or garage yourself, these steps are adapted from the CDC's disaster cleanup guidance:
Put on gloves. Don't touch the animal with bare hands.
Cover your gloved hand with a plastic trash bag, pick up the remains, turn the bag over them and seal it. Use a shovel for larger animals, then rinse it.
Call your local animal control for pickup instructions.
Wash your hands.

If it's a bat, a raccoon, or any animal a person or pet may have touched, stop. Florida's Department of Health says to contact your county health department or animal control right away, avoid further contact, and not damage the head so it can be tested. See the
CDC's guidance
